Wiring the recipe to the agentic layer is the developer responsibility, which is what keeps recipes portable if you change agent frameworks.

When the behavior is right locally, deploy the stack.

uv run socialagent bootstrap   # once per account and stage
# set whatsapp.phone_number_id in socialagent.dev.yaml, then:
uv run socialagent deploy

One step Terraform cannot do for you. AWS End User Messaging Social needs to know where to deliver inbound messages. Point your WhatsApp Business Account at the Amazon SNS topic the stack created. That setting lives on the business account, not in the stack. Point the WABA’s event destination at the stack’s SNS topic using the admin console’s Bind action, or with aws socialmessaging put-whatsapp-business-account-event-destinations from the CLI. Until it is linked, inbound messages go nowhere, and nothing errors.

When the project includes a templates.yaml, the deploy step also syncs your message templates with Meta. If you need to sync templates independently, run uv run socialagent templates sync, which reads the phone number ID and prefix from socialagent.dev.yaml and the template definitions from templates.yaml. A rejected template will fail the deploy, so fix the wording before retrying.

Meta sorts templates by purpose, and a transactional one has more permissive sending rules than a promotional one. Keep the wording plain. Emojis and marketing language are the usual reason a template gets reclassified as promotional. Running templates sync --force re-registers every template, sending approved ones back through Meta review. A plain sync skips them. Leave approved templates alone unless you need to change their content.

Now you’re ready to message your WhatsApp number.

Operate it

Shipping one bot is a project. Operating a fleet of them is the part nobody budgets for, so you also get an optional administration console with its own Terraform root. Deploy it once. Each SMART stack that sets admin_registry_bucket registers itself to a shared Amazon S3 registry on deploy, and the administration console discovers those stacks from there.

The console gives you fleet health at a glance, then per-bot depth. From a single stack view, you can do the following.

  • Read real conversations and reply by hand.
  • Inspect and cancel Amazon EventBridge schedules, and browse per-user state.
  • Restart an individual Lambda function or the runtime.
  • Review deployment history, recent errors, and Amazon CloudWatch logs.
  • Trigger test events.
  • Manage message templates with a WhatsApp-style rendering, and see a warning when Meta has reclassified one.

The console also owns the phone-number binding described earlier, so rebinding a number to a different stack is a UI action.

Sign-in runs through Amazon Cognito, with multi-factor authentication (MFA) required. Role-based permissions are then enforced on every API route. The console itself is served from Amazon CloudFront over a private Amazon S3 bucket.

The console runs on AWS services end to end. Every conversation stays within two providers: Meta and AWS. Model calls may be processed in other AWS Regions through Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference. See docs/data-flows.md in the repository for details on inference routing, media processing, and service opt-out options.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the stacks in the following order.

uv run socialagent destroy
make ui-destroy   # if you deployed the console

Terraform will not remove three things. The media and audit S3 buckets block destroy while they hold objects, unless enable_force_destroy is set. Templates registered with Meta persist. Your phone number registration is account-level and stays in place.

Get started

When building a WhatsApp AI product, the agent is where your differentiation lives. The channel integration is what eats your roadmap. SMART moves that boundary for you. Write a prompt, a few tools, and your business logic. In return you get webhook ingestion, media handling, conversation memory, scheduling, and template management. All backed by one-command infrastructure, a local development loop, and an administration console running in your own AWS account.

To go further, take the following next steps.

  • Get the code from the SMART repository on GitHub.
  • Set up your WhatsApp Business Account with AWS End User Messaging Social.
  • Start with socialagent init and socialagent dev, which need no AWS infrastructure.
  • Read the documentation in the repository for the areas this post summarized, including notifications, media handling, events and scheduling, per-user state, and message templates.
  • For further research, see the AgentCore documentation.

We would love to see what you build with it.

About the authors

item.title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMak…
item.description: Full title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations. This data helps prevent production stoppages, diagnose vehicle faults, explain drops in data-center performance, and adjust pricing as supply and demand shift. However, interpreting that data still requires specialist time, and collecting more data does not mean teams can act on it. General-purpose language models like Claude or ChatGPT can help analyze data. However, processing long histories across hundreds of operational metrics as text or images can consume large numbers of tokens, which increases cost.

To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM, an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs). These models interpret operational measurements, from equipment sensor data to supply and demand, alongside context such as maintenance records, market news, and an engineer’s observations. In doing so, TSLMs help systems recognize emerging problems in recent measurements. Experts can then ask follow-up questions to understand what changed and assess how to respond. TimeNet, the shared data infrastructure for time-series data, provides one format and API to find, build, and load the datasets used to train and evaluate these models. Together, they help organizations understand how their systems change and act before problems become costly.

OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment. This post explores how Nexthink and Aionic Labs are bringing this capability to proactive IT assistance, then shows how to deploy OpenTSLM and adapt it to your own data using TimeNet.

Figure 1. Time-series language models combine numerical measurements with text context and questions. Potential applications span physical and digital systems, with adaptation and evaluation for each task.

A customer example: Proactive IT support at Nexthink

Nexthink and Aionic Labs are building toward a digital workplace where employees get help before they need to ask for it. At the center is Spark, Nexthink’s personal IT agent, enhanced with time-series language models that connect device telemetry and context to the problems employees experience. Spark turns that understanding into action: it checks the likely issue, guides the employee through an appropriate fix, and follows up on the result. Proactive assistance becomes part of keeping work moving.

The workflow combines recent device time-series, such as CPU activity, memory use, available disk space, application stability, and connectivity, with timestamped events and device and software context. The TSLM receives the numerical measurements alongside this text context and interprets how the signals change over the observation window.

The TSLM provides Spark with three outputs:

  • State summary: Explains the likely issue and the supporting signal patterns, connecting device behavior with the employee’s experience.
  • Recommended action: Specifies checks to confirm the issue and a practical action for Spark to offer the employee.
  • Expected outcome: Describes the intended improvement and how Spark checks the result.

Device telemetry and context support investigation of a range of issues, including slow performance under high CPU or memory load, recurring application freezes or crashes, and files that fail to synchronize. Resource usage, application events, storage measurements, and connection activity provide different pieces of evidence. Combined with device configuration and software versions, they give the TSLM a broader basis for explaining the employee’s experience and directing Spark’s next checks.

In the illustrative low-disk example in Figure 2, the TSLM connects declining free space, a rising disk queue, and more frequent application hangs with likely employee symptoms, such as a slow computer or difficulty saving files. Spark checks how much space is left and whether temporary files can be removed using an IT-approved cleanup. If the checks confirm that a cleanup is appropriate, Spark shows the employee what it proposes to remove and asks for confirmation. After the employee confirms, Spark runs the cleanup, checks the space now available, and asks whether the problem has improved. If the issue persists, Spark offers to pass the findings to IT support.

TSLMs understand how systems change and help people act on that understanding. For Spark, this means recognizing emerging IT problems and guiding employees toward a solution. The same approach brings time series intelligence to manufacturing, energy, and connected products, turning measurements and context into explanations and intelligent decisions.

Figure 2. Illustrative proactive support workflow for low disk space at Nexthink. OpenTSLM generates a state summary, a recommended action, and an expected outcome from device history and context. Spark checks the device, runs an IT-approved cleanup after employee confirmation, and follows up on the result.

Solution overview

The architecture in Figure 3 provides a reusable deployment pattern for time-series applications. SageMaker JumpStart supplies the model discovery and deployment path.

SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) model hub that accelerates your ML journey. With SageMaker JumpStart, you can evaluate, compare, and deploy pretrained foundation models (FMs), including the newly available OpenTSLM model. As part of the AWS AI offerings, SageMaker JumpStart provides customizable ML solutions which you can deploy to Amazon SageMaker AI inference endpoints within your AWS infrastructure. It complements Amazon Bedrock, which offers serverless API foundation model inference along with features like customizations, knowledge bases, agents, and guardrails.

Key technical benefits of SageMaker AI and SageMaker JumpStart include:

  • Pre-built inference containers – AWS Deep Learning Containers with GPU acceleration, so you can serve the model without building your own image.
  • Automatic scaling endpoints – Managed infrastructure scales compute resources based on request volume and latency requirements.
  • Inference API – SageMaker real-time inference endpoints with standardized API calls, SDK, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration.
  • Integrated monitoring – Built-in metrics for throughput, latency, and resource utilization with an Amazon CloudWatch integration.
  • Enterprise security – Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) deployment with IAM access control and network isolation options.

The model in SageMaker JumpStart is OpenTSLM-Flamingo. It combines the Gemma 3 4B language model with a time-series encoder and cross-attention layers that let the language model attend to the encoded series. The model has 5.24 billion parameters in total, stored in bfloat16, so its weights take about 10.5 GB of GPU memory.

An application prepares numerical time series and text context, invokes the SageMaker endpoint, and receives the model’s response. The application can present that response to an expert or use it as input to another workflow.

This separation allows the application to control the observation window, select relevant signals, and validate the response before using it. It also makes the model independently adaptable: a new checkpoint can be evaluated against representative cases before the application switches to it.

In addition, we show a tutorial that fine-tunes a pretrained OpenTSLM checkpoint from Hugging Face using ARFBench data loaded through TimeNet. The notebook submits a SageMaker training job that loads ARFBench through TimeNet and fine-tunes the model. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) stores the resulting model artifact, which is then deployed to a separate SageMaker real-time inference endpoint for evaluation.

Figure 3. A reusable architecture for deploying OpenTSLM through SageMaker JumpStart and invoking it from applications that combine time-series data with text context.

Prerequisites

For the deployment walkthrough, use an AWS account with an Amazon SageMaker AI domain and a SageMaker AI execution role. The role must be able to create SageMaker models and endpoints in a supported Region, for example a role with the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy. The quick setup for single users creates both. The managed policy grants broad permissions to get started. For production, use a policy that grants only the permissions you need, as described in Amazon SageMaker AI identity-based policy examples. OpenTSLM runs on a single GPU with at least 24 GB of memory and bfloat16 support, and we recommend 32 GB of host memory. The default instance type is ml.g6.2xlarge (one NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB of memory, 32 GB of host memory). In SageMaker JumpStart, OpenTSLM also supports ml.g6.4xlarge, ml.g6.8xlarge, ml.g5.2xlarge, ml.g5.4xlarge, ml.g5.8xlarge, ml.g6e.xlarge, and ml.g6e.2xlarge. In the Service Quotas console, check your quota for “ml.g6.2xlarge for endpoint usage”, or for the instance type you choose. You need a quota of at least 1. If it’s lower, request an increase. See the OpenTSLM JumpStart model card for the model access requirements.

For fine-tuning, use JupyterLab in Amazon SageMaker Studio or a local Jupyter environment with AWS credentials configured to run the accompanying notebook, which submits the training job. The notebook uses the SageMaker default S3 bucket and an execution role. Fine-tuning runs on ml.g7e.2xlarge, so also check your quota for “ml.g7e.2xlarge for training job usage”. Training runs on the job’s managed GPU instance. The notebook itself does not need a GPU. Obtain access to the selected Hugging Face checkpoint where required.

Deploy OpenTSLM with SageMaker JumpStart

To deploy OpenTSLM in SageMaker Studio, complete the following steps:

  • In SageMaker Studio, choose Models in the navigation pane, then JumpStart models.
  • Search for “OpenTSLM” and choose OpenTSLM-Flamingo Gemma 3 4B. The model page shows the model ID, the license, and the request and response format.

Figure 4: The OpenTSLM-Flamingo Gemma 3 4B model page in SageMaker JumpStart

  • Choose Deploy.
  • On the Deploy model to endpoint form, review the Gemma Terms of Use under License agreement and select the checkbox to accept the end user license agreement (EULA). Keep the default instance type, ml.g6.2xlarge, or choose another supported instance type. Then choose Deploy.

Figure 5: The deploy model to endpoint form with the default ml.g6.2xlarge instance type and real-time inference

  • Wait until the endpoint status is InService. In our tests, this took about 6 minutes. Note the endpoint name, which starts with jumpstart-dft-. You need it to send requests and to clean up.

Figure 6: The deployed OpenTSLM endpoint with InService status in SageMaker Studio

You can also create the deployment from Python with the SageMaker Python SDK v3. The following example uses ModelBuilder. The model is gated: setting accept_eula=True accepts its license, the Gemma Terms of Use. Review the terms before you deploy. The SDK prints a link to them when it builds the model.

from sagemaker.core.helper.session_helper import get_execution_role
from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig
from sagemaker.serve.model_builder import ModelBuilder
from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute

MODEL_ID = "pytorch-reasoning-opentslm-flamingo-gemma3-4b"
INSTANCE_TYPE = "ml.g6.2xlarge"  # 1 x NVIDIA L4 (24 GB); ml.g5.2xlarge and ml.g6e.2xlarge also work
ROLE_ARN = get_execution_role()  # in SageMaker Studio; elsewhere, set your execution role ARN

builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config(
    jumpstart_config=JumpStartConfig(model_id=MODEL_ID, accept_eula=True),
    compute=Compute(instance_type=INSTANCE_TYPE),
    role_arn=ROLE_ARN,
)
builder.build(model_name="opentslm-blog-demo")
endpoint = builder.deploy(endpoint_name="opentslm-blog-demo")

Ask a question about a time series

The endpoint accepts a JSON request with one or more instances. Each instance holds a question, one or more numerical series, and optional context lines. Each series has its values, a name, and a short description of the signal, such as its unit and sampling interval. A series can hold up to 32,768 values. The endpoint scales each series to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 and passes the original mean and standard deviation to the model as text, so the model receives both the shape and the scale of the signal. Use None for a missing value. The model masks it.

Send the request with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpoint API. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to match your deployment. The calling identity needs the sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint permission. The following synthetic CPU example shows a request.

import json

import boto3

ENDPOINT_NAME = "opentslm-blog-demo"
runtime = boto3.client("sagemaker-runtime")

# One hour of CPU utilization, one sample per minute, with a five-minute spike.
cpu = [21, 20, 22, 19, 21, 20, 23, 21, 20, 19, 22, 21, 20, 21, 19, 22, 20, 21, 23, 20,
       21, 19, 20, 22, 21, 20, 19, 21, 78, 85, 82, 80, 79, 22, 20, 21, 19, 20, 22, 21,
       20, 21, 23, 19, 20, 21, 22, 20, 19, 21, 20, 22, 21, 20, 19, 21, 22, 20, 21, 20]

request = {
    "instances": [{
        "question": "Summarize the pattern and suggest what to check.",
        "series": [{
            "values": cpu,  # use None for a missing value
            "name": "CPU utilization (%)",
            "text": "CPU utilization (%), 1 sample/minute:",
        }],
        "context": ["The series covers 10:00 to 10:59 on a web server."],  # optional
    }],
    "parameters": {"max_new_tokens": 128},
}

response = runtime.invoke_endpoint(
    EndpointName=ENDPOINT_NAME,
    ContentType="application/json",
    Body=json.dumps(request),
)
print(json.loads(response["Body"].read())["generated_text"][0])

A request can hold up to four instances, each with 1 to 32 series, and the response contains one answer per instance in generated_text. max_new_tokens accepts values from 1 to 512. The model uses greedy decoding, so the same request typically returns the same answer. A real-time invocation must complete within 60 seconds, and the request body can be up to 6 MB. On ml.g6.2xlarge, the model generates about 20 tokens per second. The endpoint processes the instances of a request in sequence, so response time grows with the number of instances and the length of the answers: an answer of 512 tokens takes about 30 seconds. To stay within 60 seconds, send several instances in one request only with short answers, for example with max_new_tokens of 128. The 6 MB limit also bounds how much series data a request can carry. For long-running requests, you can use asynchronous inference.

You can send the same request with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Save the request as JSON, for example with json.dump(request, open("request.json", "w")), then run:

aws sagemaker-runtime invoke-endpoint \
    --endpoint-name opentslm-blog-demo \
    --content-type application/json \
    --body fileb://request.json \
    response.json
cat response.json

Choose an input window that preserves relevant events

OpenTSLM-Flamingo compresses the encoded time series into a fixed-size set of representations before the language model uses it. This bounds the representation passed to the language model, but it does not make the complete system unlimited in memory or guarantee that a brief event remains easy to identify in a very long recording.

Long-context research makes this distinction concrete. TS-Haystack evaluates event retrieval across recordings of different lengths and finds that the evaluated TSLM variants often lose accuracy as the history grows, especially when locating event start and end times. These results motivate testing the chosen checkpoint on the windows and questions used by your application.

Choose a window that contains the event and enough surrounding context to interpret it. For long recordings, compare overlapping windows. Preserve sampling resolution for brief events and align related channels in time. Include units, sampling interval, and the observation period in the text context. Validate both normal and abnormal examples at the intended lengths. The endpoint’s accepted payload size and the model’s useful analysis window are separate constraints.

Fine-tune OpenTSLM on ARFBench with SageMaker

Follow the accompanying fine-tuning notebook for the complete example, from preparing ARFBench data with TimeNet to launching a SageMaker training job and deploying the adapted model.

When should you fine-tune?

Start by testing the pretrained OpenTSLM model on representative examples from your application, and assess how well it answers your questions.

  • Use the pretrained model when its answers are correct and its explanations match the signals.
  • Improve the input when important information is missing, such as measurement units, sampling rate, system context, or the relevant time window.
  • Fine-tune the model when it consistently misses patterns specific to your domain or struggles with your task, even with sufficient context. Use representative signals paired with reviewed answers.

TimeNet provides a consistent way to load the data for training and evaluation. After fine-tuning, compare the adapted model with the original on examples that were not used for training.

Prepare fine-tuning data with TimeNet

ARFBench is a public benchmark of multiple-choice questions about anomalies in Datadog’s software-incident telemetry. We use ARFBench because its multiple-choice answers can be scored automatically, which makes the effect of fine-tuning measurable. The same workflow applies to tasks with open-ended answers, such as the summaries and recommended actions in the Nexthink example. TimeNet serves ARFBench as a versioned dataset: each question is stored with its answer options, its correct answer, and the metric signals. The training job loads ARFBench through TimeNet and the model checkpoint from Hugging Face.

Submit a SageMaker training job and deploy the fine-tuned model

A SageMaker training job runs the OpenTSLM training script on a GPU instance. The job fine-tunes the time-series encoder, the perceiver resampler, the cross-attention layers, and the language model’s token embeddings, and keeps the rest of the Gemma 3 language model frozen. The job saves the fine-tuned model to Amazon S3 in the layout of the Hugging Face model repository and writes the test accuracy before and after training to a metrics.json file. If your SageMaker Studio domain has a default MLflow App, the job also logs the training and validation loss and the test accuracy to it, so you can compare runs in the MLflow UI. In our run on one ml.g7e.2xlarge instance, accuracy on 135 held-out ARFBench questions rose from 5.0% to 45.9%. That is well above the 24.5% that random choice reaches on the full benchmark according to the ARFBench paper. Before fine-tuning, the model left most answers empty. Afterwards, it answered every question with one of the given options. ARFBench serves here as an example application: it shows how to adapt the model to a new task and answer format with a public dataset. The result is not a comparison with other models or an official ARFBench leaderboard result.

The following excerpt from the accompanying notebook starts the training job with ModelTrainer. scripts/train.py loads ARFBench, evaluates and fine-tunes the model, and saves it to FINETUNED_PREFIX.

trainer = ModelTrainer(
    training_image=TRAINING_IMAGE,  # the SageMaker PyTorch 2.9 training image
    source_code=SourceCode(
        source_dir="scripts", entry_script="train.py", requirements="requirements.txt"
    ),
    compute=Compute(instance_type="ml.g7e.2xlarge", volume_size_in_gb=100),
    stopping_condition=StoppingCondition(max_runtime_in_seconds=24 * 60 * 60),
    hyperparameters={"base-model": BASE_MODEL, "output": FINETUNED_PREFIX, "epochs": 3},
    role=ROLE_ARN,
)
trainer.train()

To deploy the fine-tuned model, create a new real-time endpoint on ml.g6.2xlarge, or another instance type that the JumpStart model supports, with the same container image and environment variables as the JumpStart model, and the inference script that the accompanying notebook provides. Point its model data to the S3 location of the fine-tuned model files. The request format stays the same, so you can send it the requests from the previous section. The accompanying notebook contains the code.

Adapt the workflow to your domain

The same workflow can be adapted to other time-series tasks by pairing signal windows with relevant questions and reviewed answers. Potential examples include interpreting equipment behavior with maintenance context, explaining energy-consumption patterns with operating conditions, and describing activity from wearable measurements. The data, supervision, and evaluation should reflect the domain and the decision the application is intended to support.

Preserve the timing and meaning of the measurements during preparation, and separate training and evaluation data in a way that reflects deployment. For a predictive task, only information available at prediction time belongs in the input. Domain experts should assess whether an answer is grounded in the signals and useful for the intended workflow. For free-text answers, compare them with reviewed reference answers, for example through expert ratings or LLM-as-a-judge, where a language model scores each answer against a rubric.

Clean up

Deployed endpoints continue to incur charges until you delete them. When you finish, delete the endpoint, its endpoint configuration, and its model. If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, run the following commands instead of choosing Delete on the endpoint page, which deletes only the endpoint. The commands look up the configuration and model names from the endpoint name and delete all three. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to the name of your endpoint, for example the default name that starts with jumpstart-dft- for a Studio deployment:

ENDPOINT_NAME=opentslm-blog-demo
CONFIG_NAME=$(aws sagemaker describe-endpoint --endpoint-name "$ENDPOINT_NAME" \
    --query EndpointConfigName --output text)
MODEL_NAME=$(aws sagemaker describe-endpoint-config --endpoint-config-name "$CONFIG_NAME" \
    --query 'ProductionVariants[0].ModelName' --output text)

aws sagemaker delete-endpoint --endpoint-name "$ENDPOINT_NAME"
aws sagemaker delete-endpoint-config --endpoint-config-name "$CONFIG_NAME"
aws sagemaker delete-model --model-name "$MODEL_NAME"

Repeat these commands with the name of the fine-tuned endpoint. Stop the notebook application and remove tutorial-specific S3 data and artifacts that you do not intend to retain. The training job stops when it completes.

Conclusion

Time-series language models connect numerical measurements with the questions, context, and expertise people use to make decisions. Across manufacturing, energy, wearables, and digital infrastructure, they give people and applications a common way to interpret how systems change. The broader opportunity is to connect operational history with language, making past observations more useful in current decisions.

OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy it to a real-time inference endpoint in your own AWS environment through SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker SDK. TimeNet and SageMaker training jobs provide a path to adapt the model to your domain’s signals and questions.

To get started, explore Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, follow the examples in the AWS Samples repository, and consult the OpenTSLM repository and TimeNet documentation. Start with the public ARFBench example, evaluate it on representative cases, then bring the signals, questions, and expertise from your own domain.

About the authors

item.title: Your complete guide to AWS Quick at AWS re:Invent 2026
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Your complete guide to AWS Quick at AWS re:Invent 2026

AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work, where the dashboards, agents, and automations one person creates are available to everyone on the team. Built on AWS with enterprise security and governance from the start, Quick connects to the data and applications you use every day. At AWS re:Invent 2026 (November 30 to December 4), customers including Allianz, Cox Automotive, Mondelez, DXC, and Southwest Airlines, join AWS leaders on stage to share how they govern, extend and scale Quick across their teams. Whether you’re a business or technology leader, a builder, or part of an IT, security, data, or analytics team, use this guide to find the sessions that fit your goals.

Explore the session catalog and learn more.

Keynote

Join AWS CEO Matt Garman for the re:Invent 2026 CEO Keynote on Tuesday from 8:30 AM – 10:30 AM PT as he shares the latest innovations powering the agentic era. From AI infrastructure and inference to data, agent platforms, and the software agents AWS is building, see how AWS gives you the depth, breadth, and integration to build what’s next with new announcements and stories from customers already doing it.

Can’t make it to Las Vegas? Watch 50+ sessions live on the AWS re:Invent livestream, including keynotes, talks, and labs.

Breakout sessions

Hear directly from customers about how they deployed AWS Quick, from first rollout to enterprise scale, and what they learned along the way.

BIZ216: AI assistant for public sector: Governance without compromise with AWS Quick Monday, Nov 30 | 10:00 AM PST Speakers: Rima Olinger, Sonali Sahu, Mike Shore-Nye

Public sector organizations serve diverse populations with strict boundaries: students and administrators, citizens and case workers, patients and providers. They need AI that works across these groups without compromising data isolation, compliance, or governance. Multi-tenant environments demand security frameworks most AI assistants were not built to meet. Hear from a higher education customer who faced these constraints and displaced their incumbent tool in favor of AWS Quick’s governance-first architecture: tenant-level data isolation, role-based access controls across distinct user populations, and compliance frameworks built for regulated environments. Learn why existing solutions fell short, how Quick’s native governance model met their requirements without custom engineering, and what the transition looked like from decision to deployment.

BIZ219: How a brand turned AI governance into a strategic advantage with AWS Quick Monday, Nov 30 | 10:00 AM PST Speakers: Steve Vinsik, Mark Huber, Katie Travis

In automotive, data isolation is not optional. You serve thousands of dealer clients who compete with each other, handle consumer financial data under FTC Safeguards rules, and operate across state privacy boundaries. Most AI tools cannot enforce tenant-level separation between competing dealers, restrict access by franchise agreement, or prove compliance across jurisdictions. Hear from a customer who turned that constraint into an advantage: they built a governance model with AWS Quick that enforces fine-grained data permissions across their dealer network, role-based access controls by business function, and audit frameworks that satisfy regulators and competitive separation requirements. Learn how they validated it against compliance requirements, and how governance became the reason they deployed faster than competitors still waiting on security approval.

BIZ112: From zero to 20,000 desktops: Getting started with AWS Quick Monday, Nov 30 | 12:00 PM PST Speakers: Jose Kunnackal John

Your team is drowning in context-switching: toggling between email, documents, data tools, and chat only to complete a single task. Productivity tools promise to help, but most add complexity instead of removing it. In this fireside chat, hear from customers who faced that exact challenge and deployed an AI assistant across 20,000+ users in under 90 days. Learn what convinced their leadership to invest, how they integrated AI into daily workflows without disrupting existing tools, and what the first 90 days of adoption actually looked like. Walk away with a practical roadmap for bringing AWS Quick AI assistant to your workforce at scale.

BIZ214: Empowering 200,000 people without compromising trust: AWS Quick Tuesday, Dec 1 | 4:30 PM PST Speakers: Ben Haller, Raji Sivasubramaniam, Axel Schell

Allianz needed to empower 200,000 employees with AI without sacrificing trust. With operations across dozens of regulated markets, the security, privacy, and works council requirements were non-negotiable. Every stakeholder asked the same question: how do you move fast and still earn the trust of those guarding your company’s security? Hear how Allianz partnered with AWS to deploy the capabilities that make AWS Quick enterprise-ready: protection of confidential information, structured approval workflows for agentic actions, custom branding per business unit, and multi-language support. Learn how Allianz navigated the full approval process and moved from “not yet” to “go” in six weeks.

BIZ217: One AI assistant, every data source: Unifying access with AWS Quick Wednesday, Dec 2 | 4:00 PM PST Speakers: David Provan, Jess Wang, Jesse Gebhardt

Your data lives in one platform. Your reports live in another. Your documents live somewhere else. Every time someone needs an answer, they spend time figuring out where to look before they can act. Decisions slow down. Teams duplicate work because they cannot find what already exists. New employees take months to become productive because institutional knowledge is trapped in systems they do not know how to navigate. Hear from a customer who solved this by giving their team a single AI assistant that connects across all their enterprise systems. Instead of training people on where to find information, they ask AWS Quick and get answers grounded in their real business data, regardless of where it lives. Learn how they configured the integration, how their teams adopted it, and what changed about the speed and quality of decision-making across the organization.

BIZ113: Getting started with AWS Quick: How a customer went from curious to deployed Thursday, Dec 3 | 12:00 PM PST Speakers: Leo Ohannesian, Justin Bundick, Peter Hunn

Your team spends hours on work that should take minutes: summarizing meetings, drafting documents, finding answers buried across systems, pulling data from multiple platforms. You know AI should help, but you need to see it work in a real environment before you commit. In this session, see how a customer put AWS Quick into daily workflows across their organization and watch live as it composes documents, analyzes data, summarizes conversations, and connects to enterprise systems. Hear what problems they were solving, what changed for their teams after deployment, and what surprised them about adoption. Leave with a clear picture of the problems Quick solves and how to evaluate whether it fits your organization.

BIZ213: Accelerating AI adoption and realized value with AWS Quick Thursday, Dec 3 | 1:30 PM PST Speakers: Neal Cauley, John Brock, Stefan Schulz

You deployed an AI assistant. Your team tried it for a week and stopped. The tool could not access the systems where real work happens, gave generic answers because it was disconnected from your enterprise context, and security would not approve broader rollout because the governance story was unclear. That is where most AI deployments stall. Hear from a customer who lived that exact cycle: low adoption, frustrated leadership, and a growing sense that the investment was wasted. They evaluated multiple alternatives and made the switch to AWS Quick, an AI assistant with governed access to enterprise data, native connectors to the systems their teams already use, and agentic workflows that span business units. Learn what broke in their first deployment, what they looked for in a replacement, and how governed data access turned single-digit adoption into organization-wide usage.

BIZ215: From pilot to enterprise scale with AWS Quick Thursday, Dec 3 | 4:00 PM PST Speakers: Rekha Seshadrinathan, Gayatri Ohri, Michael Murphy

Your AI pilot proved value with a small team. Now you need to deploy across the organization without a dedicated rollout team and without losing what made it work. Hear from a customer who scaled AWS Quick from an initial deployment to thousands of users across their enterprise. Learn the phased strategy they used to expand Quick’s capabilities: connecting teams to enterprise data, automating repetitive workflows, and rolling out agentic features that kept usage growing after the initial adoption wave. Discover what metrics justified continued investment and the operational model they built so scaling Quick did not create a support burden for IT. Walk away with a repeatable framework for taking AWS Quick from proof-of-concept to production deployment across your organization.

BIZ218: From AI tasks to autonomous multi-agent workflows with AWS Quick Thursday, Dec 3 | 4:00 PM PST Speakers: Ramon Lopez, Mike Hogan

The workflows that matter most in financial services span multiple systems, require multiple types of expertise, and today rely on people as the coordination layer. One person pulls data, another reviews it for compliance, a third routes it for approval. That coordination tax is where your team’s time disappears. AWS Quick changes that equation. Instead of one AI assistant doing one task, specialized agents each handle their piece and hand off to the next automatically. The human stays in the loop for judgment calls, not for data gathering and routing. Hear from a customer who moved from standalone AI use cases to compound, multi-agent workflows with AWS Quick. Learn how they identified which workflows to orchestrate first, how they designed agent handoffs that satisfy compliance, and what it means now that the coordination layer runs autonomously.

Chalk talks

Whiteboard architectures and trade-offs with the AWS Quick product and solutions teams. Bring your toughest questions.

BIZ306: Bring your own ontology: Ground AWS Quick in enterprise context Monday, Nov 30 | 10:00 AM PST Speakers: Tom Ron, Fatima Khakwani

Enterprise questions rarely have answers in a single document. Your business runs on connections: customers to products, teams to processes, and risks to regulations. But vector search doesn’t see any of that. In this chalk talk, we show how to ground AWS Quick in your enterprise context by integrating it with a knowledge graph built from your domain knowledge. We’ll walk through how we built this pattern using GraphRAG for real customers and the results they achieved. Then we’ll open the whiteboard. Bring your toughest use case and we’ll sketch your ontology live, showing how Quick would traverse it to deliver better answers.

BIZ323: Decision frameworks, evaluation, and cost management with AWS Quick Monday, Nov 30 | 10:30 AM PST Tuesday, Dec 1 | 2:30 PM PST (repeat) Speakers: Sagar Rao, Sandhya Khanderia

Moving from one agent to enterprise-wide automation means choosing the right path (Flows, Automate, Custom Agents, persistent agents) and the right trigger model. In this chalk talk, we whiteboard a decision framework that bakes in evaluation and cost management from the start, not as afterthoughts. We’ll connect orchestration across 25+ connectors, skills, and workstreams to measurable outcomes and dollars. Bring your automation backlog. You’ll leave with a decision matrix, eval harness, and a return on investment (ROI) story.

BIZ307: Architect AI-powered analytics with AWS Quick across your data platforms Monday, Nov 30 | 12:00 PM PST Speakers: Vignessh Baskaran, Jackson Dowden

As organizations adopt AI-powered analytics, they need architectures that connect business intelligence (BI) and conversational AI experiences to their existing data platforms. In this session we’ll diagram architectural patterns for connecting AWS Quick to structured data sources and integrating with third-party catalogs and semantic layers. We’ll compare the available connectivity approaches, including data sources and action connectors based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and discuss when to use each. Considerations will span production use cases like BI dashboards, embedded analytics, text-to-SQL Q&A, and agentic workflows. Together we’ll tackle real-world integration challenges including authentication, performance optimization, and governance. This session is ideal for architects and technical leaders looking to build AI-powered analytics across their data platforms.

BIZ404: Teaching Quick to remember and connect with memory and knowledge graphs Monday, Nov 30 | 1:30 PM PST Speakers: Thomas Delteil, Adi Kalyanpur

Every conversation with an AI assistant starts from scratch. Your agent doesn’t remember what worked yesterday, can’t tell you who owns a project without searching again, and repeats the same mistakes because failures are never captured. In this chalk talk, we show how AWS Quick breaks out of statelessness with two primitives: a continuous-learning memory layer where a background agent extracts reusable knowledge after each session and scores it with a probabilistic confidence model, and a personal knowledge graph that connects people, projects, decisions, and evidence across your tools so the agent has a map of your world before it reads a single document. We’ll whiteboard the architecture and the tradeoffs that shaped it, then open it up. Bring your hardest questions about memory staleness, confidence calibration, graph noise, or making agents that actually get better over time.

BIZ305: Security: Zero-trust identity and data protection in the agentic era Monday, Nov 30 | 2:30 PM PST Speakers: Priya Kakarla, Munish Gopal

Security reviews stall AI rollouts more than any capability gap, and agentic AI raises the bar. This chalk talk goes past “is it secure?” to the architecture that gets a CISO to yes. We’ll whiteboard the full identity path: single sign-on (SSO) through providers like Okta and Ping, with end-user identity propagated to the data so authorization is enforced per user, in real time, across 1P AWS and 3P sources. Then we extend that trust to agents: agent identity, deterministic policy checks on every tool call, and data protection: Purview DLP, default guardrails, deny-by-default, and full SIEM auditability.

BIZ310: Secure and scalable multi-tenant deployment patterns for AWS Quick Monday, Nov 30 | 3:00 PM PST Speakers: Chin Rane, Vineet Kachhawaha

As organizations scale their adoption of AWS Quick across business units, subsidiaries, and partner ecosystems, deploying a secure multi-tenant architecture becomes critical. This chalk talk explores proven deployment patterns that balance tenant isolation, governance, and operational efficiency when rolling out AWS Quick at enterprise scale. We will walk through two primary isolation strategies: multi-account separation using AWS Organizations for environment-level boundaries (dev/staging/prod), and namespace-based logical isolation within a single account for user-cohort segmentation.

BIZ304: Building and governing apps on Quick Monday, Nov 30 | 4:00 PM PST Speakers: Shane Thompson, Art Chan

Anyone can generate apps from a sentence. The hard part is governing them and getting them in front of the right users. This chalk talk whiteboards the full lifecycle of AWS Quick Apps: building them from natural language with no separate hosting, wiring in data and actions through MCP, and the three sharing paths: private, public URLs, and enterprise sharing gated behind admin approval workflows.

BIZ303: One context layer, every surface: Enterprise knowledge for agents that work anywhere Thursday, Dec 3 | 12:00 PM PST Speakers: Suren Raju, Josh DeMuth

Your AI agents are only as smart as the data they can reach. In most enterprises, that data is scattered across dozens of systems, siloed, ungoverned, and invisible to the agents that need it most. In this chalk talk, we architect a context layer from the ground up: connecting enterprise knowledge into a unified index, then enriching that foundation with a knowledge graph that maps organizational relationships, business rules, and domain context, giving agents permission-scoped, relationship-aware intelligence at runtime. Then we take that intelligence to where users work: browser, desktop, mobile, collaboration tools, and productivity suites. Each surface independently governed yet sharing one agent identity, one memory, and one set of guardrails. Bring your architecture. We’ll whiteboard the end-to-end path together.

Workshops

Get hands-on with AWS Quick. Bring your laptop. You’ll leave with something working.

INV001: Ctrl+Alt+Ship: Hands-On with AWS Quick, Kiro, and Amazon Connect Customer Walk-up, available all week Speakers: Michelle Koh, Anupa Bhattacharyya, Christopher Lott

Ctrl+Alt+Ship is a walk-up, self-paced lab area open all week (Nov 30 – Dec 4) in the Venetian Level 2 ballroom. No reservation is needed and workstations are provided. Attendees pick a track (Kiro, Quick or Connect) and a level, 200 or 400. Both Quick labs are business simulations where Quick connects to the company’s business systems through MCP. In the L200 Kōji Fresh lab, attendees lead the response to a product-safety crisis at a fictional Singapore food company. They investigate across email, CRM, social and supply chain, brief the board and supplier, run a recall across three systems from one instruction, and turn five data exports into board-ready charts. In the L400 SkyNova Airlines lab, 14 passengers have fallen ill overnight and an influencer is blaming the airline. Attendees use Quick across six systems to find the pattern and brief the board. They then rebook stranded passengers within a hard budget, build a Flow that runs the recovery for a grounded flight, and ship a Quick App for the airport transfer desk. Facilitators will be on hand to help.

BIZ312: Build AI-powered analytics with conversational BI on AWS Quick Tuesday, Dec 1 | 3:30 PM PST Speakers: Neeraj Kumar, Salim Khan

Construct a complete AI-powered analytics pipeline, from data ingestion to conversational consumption. Use AWS Quick’s Data Catalog to discover data, query it live without moving it into SPICE, then enrich and import metadata with semantics inherited to build natural-language Q&A. In this hands-on workshop, you start with seven raw banking tables: no catalog, no definitions. An agent inspects the data and builds the catalog for you. You ask questions in plain English and get answers. An agent generates a dashboard showing which top customers are slipping. Another agent, aware of the bank’s compliance rules, checks every offer before it ships. Then you automate the full response as a Quick Flow and wrap it in a custom app your team can use. You leave with a working banking command center that agents built, and that you can rebuild in your own account using conversational analytics.

BIZ313: Build agentic automations for business processes with AWS Quick Automate Wednesday, Dec 2 | 12:00 PM PST Speakers: Reagan Rosario, Zuhayr Raghib

In this session, learn how to build an automation using AWS Quick Automate. Through a financial services example, explore how specialized AI agents work together to handle complex interactions across web pages and business applications. You’ll create a production-ready automation featuring custom agents that use knowledge and tools to transform a merchant onboarding process. Using Quick Automate’s chat-based authoring and visual studio, you’ll configure a workflow with multiple agents, integrate with multiple tools, test and debug the workflow, and then deploy it using robust enterprise controls. Walk away knowing how to develop agentic automations for real-world use cases.

BIZ311: Master agent skills: From desktop builds to production deployment Wednesday, Dec 2 | 3:00 PM PST Speakers: Jed Lechner, Leo Mentis Raj Selvaraj

Build, govern, and scale production-ready agent skills across your enterprise on AWS Quick. Author custom skills on Quick, then shift to the admin perspective: register skills in Quick Catalog for org-wide discovery, configure access policies, and schedule autonomous execution at scale. You’ll deploy measurable automation through two business-driven use cases: churn prevention from contact center data, and intelligent claims processing that eliminates manual back-office work. Leave with working skills, a governance framework for hundreds of agents across teams, and a playbook for communicating ROI to leadership.

BIZ314: Build multi-agent workflows with AWS Quick, MCP, and AgentCore Thursday, Dec 3 | 8:30 AM PST Speakers: Vishnu Elangovan, Josh Anderson

Design and build a multi-agent system inside AWS Quick where specialized agents collaborate to automate complex business processes. Connect to enterprise systems through MCP servers on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, implement inter-agent communication, configure OAuth 2.0 authentication, and deploy autonomous workflows using Quick Flows. Modeled after production deployments running 12+ coordinated agents across enterprise resource planning (ERP), finance, and procurement, you’ll leave with a working multi-agent solution you can replicate in your own environment.

BIZ402: Configure security and governance controls for AWS Quick Thursday, Dec 3 | 12:00 PM PST Speakers: Leo Mentis Raj Selvaraj, Marshall Bunch

Implement comprehensive security and administrative controls for AWS Quick. Practice configuring identity integration, access policies, and data governance frameworks. Learn to establish monitoring, auditing, and compliance controls that meet enterprise requirements. Work through scenarios covering user management, content governance, and security best practices for AWS Quick environments in production.

Builders’ sessions

Build alongside AWS experts in small-group, code-level sessions. Bring your laptop and be ready to build.

BIZ301: Build and ship an AI-powered app with AWS Quick Monday, Nov 30 | 2:30 PM PST Speakers: Roy Yung, Oyin Oguntoye, Mei Liu, Vaidy Janardhanam, Douglas Bergquist

In this hands-on builder session, you’ll use AWS Quick to design, iterate on, and publish a fully functional application through natural-language conversation. You’ll connect to a live data source (pre-provisioned through MCP), shape your app interactively with generative AI, persist state across users, and publish something your team or customers can use immediately. Whether you’re accelerating decision-making, automating operational workflows, or putting insights directly in the hands of end users, this session shows how Quick Apps collapses the gap between having an idea and shipping a solution. Bring your laptop and be ready to build.

BIZ302: Embed AWS Quick chat agents in enterprise applications Thursday, Dec 3 | 10:00 AM PST Speakers: Arun Santhosh, Sujit Singh, Anneline Sibanda, Manasi Karale, Ashok Dasineni

Deploy a fully serverless, production-ready solution that embeds AWS Quick agents and dashboards into your enterprise web applications. Using AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), configure Amazon Cognito OAuth 2.0 authentication, AWS Lambda, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon CloudFront, and AWS WAF to create a secure embedding architecture. Implement the Quick Embedding SDK, configure domain security and token validation, and deploy a working chat agent accessible from any enterprise application, turning Quick into the conversational AI layer that meets users where they already work.

Register today to reserve a seat for our sessions.

Global AWS Quick Meetup | Kick off your week

Monday, Nov 30 | 2:30 PM – 4:30 PM PST Nomikai at the Venetian Resort

Kick off your re:Invent experience with the AWS Quick community at Nomikai, where Japanese craft meets the vibrant spirit of Las Vegas. Join us for drinks and hors d’oeuvres in a relaxed setting made for connecting.

Enjoy delicious Japanese cuisine and drinks while talking with members of the AWS Quick team, including product leaders. Get to know fellow community members, and get a preview of what’s ahead before the week gets underway. Then stay for a presentation and panel from Quick and Boomi. We can’t wait to celebrate with you. After the meetup, head to the Expo together with other community members.

Whether you’re attending AWS re:Invent 2026 in person or virtually, the AWS Quick Community is your home base for staying up to date. Explore 500+ learning resources, including weekly live online learning events, new features, demos, and Q&A.

item.title: How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant wit…
item.description: Full title: How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

This post is co-written with Mariah Miller from AWS and Colin Terry from LoanPro

Have you ever wondered what the experience is like for the person on the other end of the phone when you call your bank for support? When a borrower calls a lender, the answering agent must pull account data from dozens of fields, transaction histories, and workflow queues to orient themselves before they can help the borrower. All the while, the clock runs. Assembling that context by hand means longer calls, inconsistent service quality, and agent frustration. A loan servicing assistant built on agentic AI changes that.

LoanPro, the operating system for modern lenders, set out to change that. Working with AWS Partner AllCloud and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro built a multi-agent AI assistant that gives servicing agents immediate access to synthesized borrower context and actionable next-step recommendations. Early results show customer call times reduced by up to 15 percent, according to AllCloud’s published case study.

In this post, we walk through the business challenge, the agentic AI architecture built on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the outcomes LoanPro achieved. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with the capabilities you need to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI.

About LoanPro

LoanPro is a modern, API-first lending and credit platform that automates the entire loan lifecycle from origination to payoff. Founded in 2015, LoanPro serves as the system of record for lenders of every type: fintechs, banks and credit unions, and corporates that offer lending as a value-added service. According to LoanPro, the platform serves over 450 lenders, with loans managed on its platform reaching about 31 percent of US households. The platform powers loan management at enterprise scale across the financial services industry.

LoanPro isn’t a lender. It’s the operating system that lenders run on. That distinction matters because LoanPro’s AI strategy is designed to benefit the institutions it serves across the platform, not a single lending operation.

The challenge

One of LoanPro’s core user groups is servicing agents: the people who manage borrower accounts, handle inbound calls, process payments, and resolve issues. During a live customer interaction, an agent might need to review:

  • The borrower’s complete payment history, including missed and returned payments.
  • Active loan terms, fees, and current balance.
  • Prior interactions and open support tickets.
  • Available workflow actions such as payment plans, deferrals, or escalations.

Before the AI assistant, agents navigated this information manually, moving through multiple screens and tabs to assemble the full picture. Less experienced agents took longer, and outcomes varied depending on who picked up the phone. LoanPro needed a solution that could:

  • Instantly synthesize account data into a coherent summary.
  • Recommend the right next action based on account context.
  • Deliver more consistent servicing quality across agents of different experience levels.

Solution overview

With the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro partnered with AllCloud to design and build a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock. The assistant runs on Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock (see Models at a glance in Amazon Bedrock). Model availability varies by AWS Region. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models in Amazon Bedrock. It’s orchestrated with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Agent logic is built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source framework for building AI agents with tool use. The system coordinates specialized agents through a composer that routes each request to the right specialist, so each agent handles a focused task and can be evaluated and improved independently. The team chose these managed services over building the agent runtime and model access in-house. Amazon Bedrock provides access to leading foundation models through a single API, giving the team flexibility to adopt new models without managing separate endpoints. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides a managed agent runtime that removes the operational overhead of running agents in production.

Figure 1 shows this flow in implementation terms. A user request enters through LoanPro API v2 on Amazon API Gateway. An AWS Lambda handler places the request on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The Agent Interceptor Lambda function then invokes the Loan Summary Agent. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and uses Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. It reaches its tools through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The gateway finds the right tool in a catalog that the Loan Summary Service registers in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The Loan Summary Tool Lambda function validates the caller’s signature against LoanPro’s single sign-on (SSO) service. It then retrieves account data from LoanPro’s loan management system, which runs on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) behind a Network Load Balancer. The system’s role-based access controls validate the same signature. LoanPro also checks each request against the user’s permissions and compliance controls, then writes the action to its audit trail. The sections that follow describe these pieces: the multi-agent system, the tools it calls, and the gateway.

Figure 1: High-level architecture of the LoanPro AI servicing assistant

The architecture has four key components, which combine the pieces in Figure 1 with the composer agent and Invoke API Tool that coordinate and act on them:

Multi-agent architecture with Strands Agents SDK

The solution uses a multi-agent architecture built with the Strands Agents SDK. Rather than a single monolithic model handling every task, specialized agents collaborate to serve different parts of the servicing workflow. One agent focuses on data retrieval and account summarization. Another handles action selection and workflow recommendations. A composer agent routes each request to the right specialist and composes the final response. This separation of concerns makes each agent more straightforward to evaluate, tune, and extend independently.

Tool use: Data Retrieval and Invoke API

The agents retrieve borrower data from LoanPro’s internal systems through tool use, a capability in Amazon Bedrock for calling external functions and APIs. Two primary tools power the assistant:

  • Data Retrieval Tool: Fetches account details, payment histories, loan terms, and borrower metadata from LoanPro’s data layer, shown in Figure 1 as the Loan Summary Tool. It spans eight distinct API endpoints, synthesizing around 1,400 fields per account.
  • Invoke API Tool: Triggers workflow actions within LoanPro’s platform, such as presenting informational panels to the agent or initiating a predefined automation sequence.

By connecting to LoanPro’s existing APIs, the assistant works with live production data without requiring a separate data pipeline or data warehouse.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with AWS Lambda

AgentCore Gateway is the secure access layer between the agents and the tools they call. It exposes LoanPro’s APIs to the agents as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), handles authentication, and manages those connections. AWS Lambda, a serverless compute service that runs code without provisioning or managing servers, provides the integration layer between the gateway and LoanPro’s APIs. The team chose AgentCore Gateway with Lambda over a direct integration for three reasons. It centralizes authentication at a managed entry point, isolates LoanPro’s APIs behind a managed boundary, and lets new tools be added without redeploying the agents. This serverless approach keeps the infrastructure lightweight and scales automatically with request volume. In Figure 1, the Agent Interceptor (an AWS Lambda function) invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime. AgentCore Gateway enforces this access control, screening each request before it reaches the Loan Summary Tool. Because the assistant operates in a regulated lending context, the production deployment pairs these components with additional controls. LoanPro’s role-based access controls and compliance guardrails apply to each request, and AI actions are written to LoanPro’s audit trail and attributed to a named, responsible person.

Integration into LoanPro’s existing web portal

The assistant is embedded directly into LoanPro’s existing web portal, the same interface servicing agents already use. Agents interact with the AI assistant through two components:

  • Account summary view: When an agent opens a borrower account, the assistant automatically generates a narrative summary of the account’s health, recent activity, and outstanding issues. Raw data becomes a coherent story about the borrower’s situation.
  • Conversational chat interface: Agents can ask follow-up questions in natural language to dig deeper into specific account details. The team describes this as allowing agents to “talk to the loan.” Every agent interaction with the chat interface is logged, maintaining an auditable record of actions taken during a borrower conversation.

Implementation approach

LoanPro built the assistant with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, which pairs AWS applied scientists with customers and partners to accelerate generative AI initiatives, and AllCloud, an AWS Premier Consulting Partner. The three teams designed and built the solution together. What began as a focused engagement now runs in production, serving LoanPro’s servicing agents.

The work was organized into two parallel workstreams:

Workstream 1: Servicing agent assistant

The primary workstream built the AI assistant that is now running in production. Key activities included:

  • Selecting and mapping the data sources (application data, loan histories, borrower records) the agent would need to retrieve.
  • Developing agent functionality for autonomous data retrieval and intelligent action selection.
  • Iterating on prompts to improve retrieval accuracy and output quality.
  • Documenting LoanPro’s security model and integration patterns to inform the production roadmap.

Workstream 2: LLM account rule automation advisory

LoanPro had an existing proof of concept (POC) that used a large language model (LLM) to convert natural language into rule automation code for their Clojure rules engine. The core functionality worked, but the solution had known limitations: frequent timeouts, no monitoring, and no deployment strategy. AllCloud conducted architectural reviews and provided recommendations to bring this existing POC to a production-ready state, including a documented production architecture and risk assessment.

Evaluation pipeline

A structured evaluation pipeline validated agent accuracy against benchmarks established by LoanPro’s subject-matter experts (SMEs). The team assembled a benchmark of 150 SME-labeled accounts. Against that benchmark, they measured the agent’s ability to retrieve data, summarize findings, and select appropriate actions, holding it to a 99 percent accuracy target that the agent met. This framework carries forward into production, giving LoanPro a repeatable process for measuring and improving agent performance over time.

Results

Deploying the AI assistant delivered measurable operational impact:

  • Up to 15 percent reduction in customer call times (source: AllCloud case study). Across over 800 servicing professionals at LoanPro’s early launch lender partners, agents previously spent 18–20 percent of every call (1–2.5 minutes across 5–7 clicks) orienting to accounts. The AI assistant consolidates that context into a single click, saving 1 to nearly 2 minutes per call. Across those agents, that reclaims up to 9 minutes per operating hour per agent, roughly 120 hours of agent capacity every operating hour.
  • Decreased internal ticket volumes by nearly 8 percent (source: LoanPro). Lenders on the platform report fewer support escalations as agents resolve more cases during the initial call.
  • Account summaries in under 15 seconds (source: LoanPro internal benchmarks). The narrative summary transforms raw borrower data into a coherent account story within 15 seconds of opening an account, replacing what previously took agents 3–5 minutes of manual navigation.
  • Consistent servicing quality. The assistant provides the same level of account context and action recommendations to agents across the platform, reducing variability tied to individual experience levels.
  • Compliance-aligned interaction logging. Every action and query the agent makes through the AI assistant is logged, providing an auditable record of interactions during borrower conversations.
  • Responsible AI controls. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content filtering and grounding validation to agent responses alongside LoanPro’s compliance guardrails and role-based access controls (RBAC), keeping outputs within policy before they reach a servicing agent and the borrower.
“The AI assistant has changed how servicing agents work. Instead of spending the first few minutes of every call navigating screens and assembling context, agents now open an account and immediately see the full picture with prescriptive recommendations around the next actions to take. That time savings compounds across thousands of calls.”
— Colin Terry, Chief Product Officer, LoanPro

Looking ahead

Building on the success of the servicing agent assistant, LoanPro and AllCloud are expanding their collaboration. The teams are developing additional AI agents to extend intelligent capabilities across more parts of the lending workflow, moving beyond servicing into areas such as collections and origination support.

The modular, multi-agent architecture makes this expansion practical. New agents can be built and deployed independently using the same Amazon Bedrock AgentCore infrastructure, without redesigning the core system. As the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore continue to evolve, LoanPro plans to incorporate new capabilities as they become available.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how LoanPro, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, and AllCloud built a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help servicing agents resolve borrower calls faster and more consistently. The solution retrieves data autonomously, generates account summaries in real time, and recommends next-best actions, reducing customer call times by up to 15 percent.

If you are building agentic AI solutions for customer-facing workflows, here are some resources to explore:

  • Amazon Bedrock: Fully managed service for building with foundation models.
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Infrastructure to deploy, manage, and scale AI agents.
  • Strands Agents SDK: Open source framework for building AI agents with tool use.
  • AWS Generative AI Innovation Center: Accelerate your generative AI journey with AWS experts.

To get started, explore the Strands Agents SDK on GitHub for building multi-agent systems, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation for deploying agents at scale, or visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center to learn how AWS experts can help accelerate your own AI initiative.

About the authors

item.title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform…
item.description: Full title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams

Companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use. The nondeterministic nature of generative AI models introduces a complexity that previous software development practices didn’t anticipate. Consider a real estate app that generates property listings from retrieved data: does it accurately reflect the property, or hallucinate features that don’t exist? Or a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases: can you verify that it doesn’t surface confidential information?

Until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference. Models didn’t reason, use tools, or take actions. When the conversation extended to model-powered systems, it covered statistically bounded situations you could test against known inputs. Generative AI powered applications and agents changed this. The systems now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, expanding both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover.

Organizations are turning Responsible AI, which includes the pillars of security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance into a growth strategy by addressing its expanding scope early. When enterprises adopt agentic AI at scale, the positive and negative impacts come hand in hand. As Wade and Wirtz observe in the Harvard Business Review, trust is becoming a competitive differentiator. The same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate, and organizations that govern them earn stakeholder confidence. Robinhood, for example, built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance. They achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. Structuring these practices across platform maturity is the next step. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Application teams. Application teams, sometimes called Workstream teams, build and own agents on the platform.

This post provides a condensed, actionable roadmap for the Platform team and Application teams building on agentic AI. It’s designed to be read together: the Platform team sets up the guardrails. Application teams build within them. Both need a shared language for where they are and what good looks like. We provide a Responsible AI Assessment Skill, that maps the AWS Responsible AI Lens pillars to a three-phase maturity model: governance foundations, pilot deployment, and evaluation and hardening. For each phase, it shows which responsible AI pillars are critical and when to revisit them. An accompanying scorecard lets both application teams and the platform team assess where they are today and iterate as their applications mature.

Note: This post covers the key questions to ask at each phase. It leaves out step-by-step implementation details. This post also doesn’t provide legal or compliance advice. Always consult your legal team.

The challenge

In conversations with customers building agentic AI platforms, four challenges surface consistently.

  • Unpredictable runtime behavior: nondeterministic outputs, goal drift, and cascading failures where one agent error propagates across services. A financial services company in Germany found that multi-agent orchestration amplified a single misclassification into policy violations across three downstream services.
  • Data exposure and authority boundaries: Scope every agent to its intended tenants, data, systems, and actions. Isolate session context so each session starts with data residency at the access layer, and grant privileged access through least-privilege, task-bound permissions that agents can’t modify themselves. Agents then act only in the systems and with the authority they were explicitly given.
  • Regulatory velocity: EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, and upcoming legislation are creating compliance requirements faster than governance can adapt. Proving compliance for nondeterministic systems requires continuous evaluation, which should be monitored and revisited with a predefined cadence (for example, daily, weekly, or monthly).
  • Team collaboration: organizations lack a shared framework defining who owns what across the agent lifecycle. A media company in the UK flagged that segregation of duty between developer and deployment teams is undefined for agent workloads. The Platform team builds guardrails that application teams work around, and application teams defer responsibility they assume the platform handles.

Figure 1: Agentic AI platforms introduce novel challenges regarding responsible AI.

Solution: A three-phase responsible AI maturity framework

In this post, we define an agentic AI platform as described in AgentOps: Operationalize agentic AI at scale with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a system for building, deploying, and operating AI agents securely at scale, covering governance, build and operations, evaluation, and observability. Your responsible AI posture should mature progressively alongside this platform. We break the journey into three phases and present prioritized responsible AI pillars across a customizable 12-week implementation timeline, allowing the platform team to establish a solid responsible AI foundation while their first use cases take shape.

Figure 2: Overview of the proposed responsible AI maturity framework for agentic AI platforms. Teams integrate responsible AI over three phases.

Phase 1: Governance foundation

Focus pillars: Governance, security and privacy

In this phase, assess project fit, risks, and ethics, secure legal and compliance approvals, and define the trust model for AI agents. The application teams classify risks for each planned use case using a risk rubric. The Platform team focuses on establishing the core landing zone infrastructure, for example, setting up the overarching monitoring and access control, and governing newly onboarded agents and use cases from the start.

Critical tasks to consider in this phase include:

Security and privacy

  • Evaluate access to data and systems needed by each agent and assess potential impact. This lays the foundation for the knowledge grounding strategy.
  • Implement foundational data security and data exfiltration protection with data classification, data access control, logging, data integrity, and data access monitoring.
  • Build a map of the data that is shared between agents like organizational knowledge bases and the subjective data like context graphs which individual agents might need. Then establish access boundaries and assign read/write permissions accordingly.

Governance

  • Define a risk classification rubric aligned to your regulatory obligations (EU AI Act risk tiers, financial services industry requirements, and so on). Assign Low / Medium / High / Unacceptable risk levels to each planned use case and document the control requirements each risk level triggers. Gather relevant documentation and traceability requirements.
  • Before onboarding agents, the underlying models need to go through a vetting procedure. The procedure covers a series of evaluations with safety and reliability criteria. Catalog approved models based on capability, latency, and cost.
  • Implement a process to centrally register and govern products like agents, shared tools and skills deployed in your organization for centralized visibility and consumption. Every product gets registered with owner, risk tier, and regulatory scope. If a resource (agent, tool, skill) isn’t in the registry, it can’t be discovered and managed by the organization.

Phase 2: Pilot deployment

Focus pillars: Safety, veracity and robustness, controllability, security and privacy

Deploy your first agent that serves measurable business value. With the template and developer guidance provided from the Platform team, application teams implement orchestration patterns, memory, guardrail baselines, knowledge grounding, and tool use patterns. Risks identified in the foundation phase must now be addressed through a set of concrete controls in a pilot implementation.

In this phase, application teams consider the following concerns:

Safety

  • Guardrails. Platform team establishes foundational personally identifiable information (PII) redaction filters for model I/O and tool calls. Provide a set of guardrails rules ready to be applied. Application teams then set content moderation thresholds explicitly based on the use case the agent serves. Configure human escalation for low-confidence responses.
  • Policies. Define which agent can access what tool and how. Augment with fallback scenarios in case of policy violations.

Veracity and robustness

  • Knowledge grounding with checks: Even with the right context, models can still hallucinate or misrepresent the provided sources. Therefore, configure contextual grounding checks to verify every response is correctly grounded in relevant data. For regulated use cases, activate automated reasoning for verifiable outputs. Implement a process to curate and update your knowledge sources. Define how out-of-domain requests are classified and handled.

Controllability
